content: Stretch marks, also known as striae in dermatological terminology, are a type of scarring that appears on the skin with a silvery-white coloration. These marks result from the tearing of the dermis, the middle layer of the skin, and while they may fade over time, they do not completely disappear. Stretch marks are commonly associated with rapid skin stretching, which occurs during periods of rapid growth, such as puberty, or significant weight gain, such as during pregnancy. Although the skin is naturally elastic, excessive and rapid stretching can lead to permanent stretch marks. In medical terms, these marks are referred to as striae distensae, striae atrophicae, or striae gravidarum when related to pregnancy. Other terms include lineae atrophicae and linea albicante. Initially, stretch marks appear as reddish or purplish lines on the skin. Over time, they fade to a lighter, silvery hue. The affected areas often feel soft and appear empty upon touch. The human skin consists of three layers: the epidermis (outermost layer), the dermis (middle layer), and the subcutaneous stratum (innermost layer). Stretch marks form in the dermis, which is responsible for maintaining the skin's shape and resilience. The formation of stretch marks is influenced by the direction and location of skin stretching, but stretching alone is not the sole cause. These marks can develop anywhere on the body but are most commonly found in areas where fat is stored, such as the abdomen (especially near the navel), breasts, upper arms, underarms, thighs (both inner and outer), hips, and buttocks. While stretch marks do not pose any health risks or impair the body's ability to function or repair itself, they are often a cosmetic concern. The development of stretch marks is influenced by glucocorticoid hormones, which interfere with the production of collagen and elastin fibers by fibroblasts in the skin. Collagen and elastin are essential for maintaining the skin's elasticity and strength during rapid growth. A deficiency in these supportive fibers leads to tearing of the dermis and epidermis. If the damage extends through both the dermis and epidermis, treatments such as laser therapy cannot completely remove the stretch marks. During pregnancy, between 75% and 90% of women develop stretch marks to some degree, typically appearing in the sixth or seventh month due to sustained hormonal changes. Research on the prevention of stretch marks is limited. One randomized controlled study found that daily application of a cream containing Centella asiatica extract, vitamin E, and collagen-elastin hydrolysates (Trofolastin) was associated with fewer stretch marks during pregnancy. Another study, though lacking a placebo control, suggested that a cream containing vitamin E, panthenol, hyaluronic acid, elastin, and menthol (Verum) reduced the incidence of stretch marks compared to no treatment. However, there is no evidence to support the effectiveness of cocoa butter in preventing or improving stretch marks. Various treatments are available to improve the appearance of existing stretch marks. These include laser treatments, dermabrasion, and prescription retinoids. When used daily for one month, retinoids have shown significant improvement in the length, depth, and surface irregularity of stretch marks. Some manufacturers claim that the best results are achieved on newer stretch marks, but there is limited evidence to support this. A study published in Dermatologic Surgery demonstrated that combining radiofrequency with 585-nm pulsed dye laser treatment resulted in good to very good improvement in 89.2% of 37 patients, though further research is needed. Pulsed dye lasers, however, may increase pigmentation in individuals with darker skin tones after repeated treatments. Surgical options, such as abdominoplasty (tummy tuck), can remove stretch marks located on the lower abdomen by excising the skin below the navel. Fractional laser resurfacing is a newer treatment modality that targets stretch marks by delivering scattered pulses of light to a fraction of the affected area during each session. This approach creates microscopic wounds, stimulating the production of new collagen and epithelium without significant downtime. A 2007 clinical trial reported up to 75% improvement in stretch marks after 5-6 treatments. Additionally, a Brazilian study demonstrated that fractional photothermolysis (Fraxel) improved the texture and appearance of mature, white stretch marks in patients with skin types I-IV.
